common_name: Pink Triumph Nerine (Large-Flowered Hardy Guernsey Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in spring in very well-drained, lean soil in full sun.

directions: Set bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in gritty, sharply drained, lean soil in full sun, ideally sheltered by a warm wall in the coldest part of its range. Pink Triumph is a robust selection of the hardiest nerine species, bearing large, lily-like heads of mid-pink, wavy-petaled flowers with a deeper pink eye toward the center of each bloom, opening on bare stems from September into November ahead of the strap-shaped leaves. Once established, leave clumps undisturbed for years and withhold summer water during the bulb's dry dormancy, since flowering is best when bulbs are slightly congested. Where winters run colder or wetter than zone 7 allows, grow in pots that can be moved under cover or mulch heavily each fall.

common_name: Lilacea Tiger Flower (Lilac Peacock Tiger Flower)

planting.note: Plant bulbs after all frost danger passes in spring, once soil has warmed above 60°F.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 in deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; 'Lilacea' bears three large, vivid lilac-purple outer petals surrounding a smaller central cup of soft yellow densely speckled with red, a cooler-toned counterpart to the orange and yellow forms of the species. Each exotic bloom lasts only a single day, but an established clump produces a long succession of new flowers through mid- to late summer. Plant bulbs in generous drifts of a dozen or more for the best display, and in zones colder than 8, lift bulbs after the first frost, dry thoroughly, and store in a cool, frost-free place over winter.

common_name: Speciosa Tiger Flower (Red Peacock Tiger Flower)

planting.note: Plant bulbs after all frost danger passes in spring, once soil has warmed above 60°F.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 in deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; 'Speciosa' is a richly colored form of tiger flower with intense red outer petals opening around a yellow-throated central cup that is heavily marked with darker red spots, one of the boldest and most saturated color forms of the species. Individual flowers open for only a single day apiece, but vigorous clumps keep producing new blooms through the height of summer. Group bulbs generously for maximum impact, and in climates colder than zone 8, dig and dry the bulbs after frost kills the foliage, storing them frost-free for replanting the following spring.

common_name: Canariensis Tiger Flower (Pale Yellow Peacock Tiger Flower)

planting.note: Plant bulbs after all frost danger passes in spring, once soil has warmed above 60°F.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 in deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; 'Canariensis' opens large, pale canary-yellow outer petals around a smaller central cup marked with red spotting, a soft, muted counterpart to the more saturated golden tones of 'Aurea'. Like other tiger flower forms, each three-petaled bloom lasts a single day, with established clumps producing a steady run of new flowers from midsummer into early fall. Plant in bold groups of a dozen or more bulbs for the best show, and where winters are colder than zone 8, lift bulbs after frost, dry them, and store in a frost-free spot for replanting in spring.

common_name: Immaculata Tiger Flower (Pure White Unspotted Peacock Tiger Flower)

planting.note: Plant bulbs after all frost danger passes in spring, once soil has warmed above 60°F.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 in deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; 'Immaculata' arose as a sport of the white-flowered 'Alba' and is distinguished from it by flowers of uniform snowy white with none of the red speckling that marks the central cup of 'Alba' and the species, occasionally showing a faint green or creamy tint instead. Each bloom opens for only a single day, but an established clump keeps up a long succession of flowers through mid- to late summer. Plant in generous drifts for best display, and in zones colder than 8, lift bulbs after the first frost, dry thoroughly, and store frost-free over winter.

common_name: Rosea Tiger Flower (Rose-Pink Peacock Tiger Flower)

planting.note: Plant bulbs after all frost danger passes in spring, once soil has warmed above 60°F.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 in deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; 'Rosea' bears three large rose-pink outer petals with soft yellow at their base, surrounding a smaller speckled central cup, giving a warmer, more delicate color than the plain species. Individual flowers open for a single day each, but a well-grown clump produces a continuous run of new blooms across mid- to late summer. Set bulbs in bold groups for the best effect, and where winters are colder than zone 8, dig and dry bulbs after frost blackens the foliage, storing them frost-free for replanting the next spring.

common_name: Alba Two-Tone Pineapple Lily (White-Flowered Pineapple Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs about 6 in deep after last frost in fertile, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun; mulch well over winter in the coldest end of its range.

directions: Plant bulbs roughly 6 in deep after last frost in fertile, humus-rich, well-drained soil in a sheltered, full-sun spot, mulching well in colder areas. 'Alba' is a plain white-flowered form of the two-tone pineapple lily, lacking the purple margins of the typical form and instead sending up a dense, creamy-white flower spike topped with a tuft of leafy bracts resembling a pineapple crown, rising above wavy-edged, semi-erect, strap-shaped leaves. It can be distinguished from the similar Eucomis autumnalis by its notably longer flower stalks. Water regularly through summer growth, taper off as the foliage yellows in fall, and mulch heavily or lift and store bulbs where winters are harsher than zone 7.

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average to sandy soil in full sun; in colder zones, plant in spring instead and lift for winter storage.

directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in well-drained, average to sandy soil in full sun. Stanford Scarlet is a well-proven, long-cultivated hybrid watsonia forming clumps of sword-shaped, iris-like leaves from which tall, unbranched stems rise in summer, each bearing up to a dozen tubular, vivid scarlet-red flowers opening in succession from the base of the spike upward. Its brilliant color and imposing height make it a striking accent among South African summer bulbs or a standout cut flower. Let corms multiply undisturbed for several years for the fullest display, and where winters are colder than zone 8, lift corms after the foliage dies back and store them dry until spring.

common_name: Tresco Hybrid Watsonia (Isles of Scilly Bugle Lily)

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average to sandy soil in full sun; in colder zones, plant in spring instead and lift for winter storage.

directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in well-drained, average to sandy soil in full sun. Tresco Hybrids are a tender, semi-evergreen strain of watsonia originally raised on Tresco in the Isles of Scilly, forming narrow clumps of upright, grey-green, sword-shaped leaves topped in summer by erect spikes of tubular flowers ranging through shades of pink, salmon, and orange on a single planting grown from seed. Because seedling color varies, grow a group for a naturally mixed, informal display rather than a uniform color block. Being more tender than many South African watsonias, it needs the mildest available winters or protected culture; where winters are colder than zone 9, lift corms in fall and store them dry, frost-free, until spring.
